items.followUp: Why are viruses considered obligate intracellular parasites?

rubric.why: Shows that viruses are not made of cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that viruses are not made of cells or lack cellular organization.

rubric.why: Identifies the viral structure or explains why viruses depend on a host.
rubric.description: A virus consists of genetic material and a protein coat, and can reproduce only inside a living host cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either the basic structure or dependence on a host cell for replication.

modelAnswer: Viruses are acellular because they are not made of cells and lack cellular organization.
They consist of genetic material enclosed in a protein coat and can reproduce only inside a living host cell.

items.followUp: State one difference between a virus and a bacterium in cellular organization.

rubric.why: Correctly recognizes that the two terms usually refer to the same structure.
rubric.description: “Plasma membrane” and “cell membrane” are generally names for the same membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the terms are synonymous or refer to the same membrane.

rubric.why: Adds a correct description of the membrane’s position or function.
rubric.description: The membrane surrounds the protoplasm and controls movement of substances into and out of the cell; in plants it lies inside the cell wall.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct location or function.

modelAnswer: Plasma membrane and cell membrane are generally two names for the same structure, so they are not different membranes.
It surrounds the protoplasm, is selectively permeable, and in a plant cell lies just inside the cell wall.

items.followUp: Define osmosis and state whether it is an active or passive process.

rubric.why: Identifies diffusion as movement of particles.
rubric.description: Diffusion is the movement of particles or molecules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying particle or molecule movement.

rubric.why: Includes the direction of movement or that the process requires no cellular energy.
rubric.description: Particles move from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration without using energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the concentration direction and/or energy-free nature.

modelAnswer: Passive diffusion is the movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
It occurs down the concentration gradient without the use of cellular energy.

items.followUp: What is the difference between chromosomes in a parent cell and daughter cells after mitosis?

rubric.why: Identifies karyokinesis as division of the nucleus or its chromosomes.
rubric.description: Karyokinesis is division of the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining karyokinesis as nuclear division.

rubric.why: Identifies cytokinesis as division of the cytoplasm.
rubric.description: Cytokinesis is division of the cytoplasm to form separate daughter cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining cytokinesis as cytoplasmic division.

modelAnswer: Karyokinesis is the division of the nucleus.
Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm, which separates the daughter cells.

items.followUp: How does cytokinesis occur in an animal cell?

rubric.why: Identifies the structure that begins plant-cell cytokinesis.
rubric.description: A cell plate forms at the middle of the cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a cell plate forms in the centre.

rubric.why: Explains how the plate separates the daughter cells.
rubric.description: The cell plate grows outward and joins the existing cell wall, separating the two daughter cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing outward growth and separation, or the resulting partition.

modelAnswer: In a plant cell, a cell plate forms in the middle of the cell between the two daughter nuclei.
The cell plate grows outward and joins the existing cell wall, separating the cell into two daughter cells.

items.followUp: Explain the role of mitosis in wound healing.

rubric.why: Connects mitosis with production of new cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that mitosis produces new cells by cell division.

rubric.why: Explains how the new cells contribute to regeneration.
rubric.description: The new cells replace lost or damaged cells and help restore tissues or body parts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the new cells to replacement or restoration.

modelAnswer: Mitosis produces new cells by cell division.
These cells replace lost or damaged cells and help restore tissues or body parts during regeneration.

rubric.why: Defines metabolism as the totality of reactions in an organism.
rubric.description: Metabolism is the sum of all chemical or biochemical reactions occurring in an organism.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the idea of the total or sum of reactions.

rubric.why: Places the reactions in the organism or its cells.
rubric.description: These reactions occur in the living organism or its cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for locating the reactions in a living organism or its cells.

modelAnswer: Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions occurring in the cells of a living organism.

items.followUp: What happens to the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction when substrate concentration keeps increasing after saturation?

rubric.why: Defines saturation in terms of enzyme active sites being occupied.
rubric.description: Saturation occurs when all enzyme active sites are occupied by substrate molecules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that all active sites are occupied.

rubric.why: States the consequence of active-site saturation for reaction rate.
rubric.description: The reaction rate has reached its maximum and does not increase further when more substrate is added.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the rate is maximal or no longer increases.

modelAnswer: Saturation of active sites occurs when all the active sites of enzyme molecules are occupied by substrate molecules.
The reaction rate then reaches its maximum and does not increase further by adding more substrate.
